# Results

100 proven results with stable IDs and 3 conditional results (proven under hypotheses that are named Lean propositions). An ID is never reused; a withdrawn result is kept as `retired`. Every declaration of the library, and so every proven result, depends only on the axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

Tier: **established** (standard mathematics and physics that the frontier work needs; candidates for Mathlib or Physlib later); **frontier** (proposals published in the peer-reviewed literature, labelled as proposals); **exploratory** (new or unpublished models and conjectures, kept in `Exploratory/` folders that nothing else imports; promoted to frontier only after publication). Every result is about the mathematics of a model, not a claim that the model describes nature.

Review: every entry is **kernel-checked**: Lean's kernel verified the proof (for a stated target, that the statement is well-formed). A kernel check guarantees the proof, not that a statement or a definition means what its source means. An entry that a domain expert has compared with its source is marked **human-reviewed**, with a link to the issue that holds the review. To review an entry, or to report that a statement does not match its source, open an issue that names the entry's ID.

## SL(2,ℂ) and its unitary principal series

API map: [Lightlike/Lorentz/API-map.md](../Lightlike/Lorentz/API-map.md)

| ID | Result | Status | Tier | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LL-0014 | SL(2,ℂ) is unimodular | proven | established | `Lightlike.Lorentz.SL2C.haar_isMulRightInvariant` in [SL2C.lean](../Lightlike/Lorentz/SL2C.lean) |
| LL-0015 | The principal series of SL(2,ℂ) is a unitary representation | proven | established | `Lightlike.Lorentz.principalSeries_mem_unitary`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.principalSeries_mul` in [PrincipalSeries.lean](../Lightlike/Lorentz/PrincipalSeries.lean) |
| LL-0016 | The Casimirs of the principal series (k, ρ) are k² − ρ² − 1 and kρ | proven | established | `Lightlike.Lorentz.casimir1_eq`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.casimir2_eq` in [Homogeneous.lean](../Lightlike/Lorentz/Homogeneous.lean) |
| LL-0017 | The principal series (k, ρ) restricted to SU(2) is the direct sum of the spins |k| + ℓ, each once | proven | established | `Lightlike.Lorentz.principalSeries_isHilbertSum`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.intertwiner_eq_smul` in [SU2Decomposition.lean](../Lightlike/Lorentz/SU2Decomposition.lean) |
| LL-0046 | The Lorentzian EPRL vertex amplitude is finite for every Immirzi parameter, all spins and every coefficient array (see note) | proven | frontier | `Lightlike.Lorentz.integrable_eprlIntegrand`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.lintegral_enorm_eprlIntegrand_lt_top`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.eprlVertex_eq_integral`, `Lightlike.Lorentz.integrable_linkProd_inner` in [EPRL.lean](../Lightlike/Lorentz/EPRL.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-0046.** Labels k = j and ρ = γ(j + 1), in Ding and Rovelli's form; Engle–Pereira's ρ = γj in this normalisation (ρ = 2γj in theirs). One of the five integrations is dropped (V₄ = 1), as in Engle–Pereira. The coefficients are arbitrary arrays, contracted without the ε twist on the bra legs, so invariant intertwiners are covered as special arrays, but equality with Engle–Pereira's amplitude on invariant intertwiners is not proven. The proof uses only the decay of the vectors, so finiteness holds for every choice of labels. Non-vacuity is shown at spin 0 for γ in some neighbourhood of 0. The amplitude is defined up to the normalisation of the Haar measure.

| LL-0025 | The Ponzano–Regge weight and the cutoff amplitude are invariant under the 2-3 move, with the new edge summed over all its spins | proven | frontier | `Lightlike.PR.weight_move23_unconditional`, `Lightlike.PR.amplitude_move23_unconditional` in [Unconditional.lean](../Lightlike/PonzanoRegge/Unconditional.lean) |

| LL-0027 | The cutoff gauge-fixed Ponzano–Regge amplitude (spin 0 on the gauge set, finite cutoffs on the other edges) is unchanged along chains of 2-3, 1-4 and recut steps (see note) | proven | frontier | `Lightlike.PR.amplitudeGF_eqvGen`, `Lightlike.PR.amplitudeGF_eqvGen_tree` in [GaugeFixed.lean](../Lightlike/PonzanoRegge/GaugeFixed.lean) |
| LL-0028 | The gauge-fixed amplitude does not depend on the maximal tree under triangle exchanges | proven | frontier | `Lightlike.PR.amplitudeGF_exchange`, `Lightlike.PR.amplitudeGF_eqvGen_exchange` in [GaugeChange.lean](../Lightlike/PonzanoRegge/GaugeChange.lean) |
| LL-0029 | The 3D Pachner moves preserve closed combinatorial 3-manifolds (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PR.isCombManifold_move23_iff`, `Lightlike.PR.isCombManifold_move14_iff`, `Lightlike.PR.isCombManifold_iff_of_eqvGen` in [Manifold.lean](../Lightlike/PonzanoRegge/Manifold.lean) |
| LL-0030 | The Ponzano–Regge asymptotic formula for the 6j symbol (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.Asymptotics.ponzanoReggeFormula` in [SaddleAssembly.lean](../Lightlike/Asymptotics/SaddleAssembly.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-0027.** An identity at finite cutoff. Independence of the gauge tree in general and removal of the cutoff are not proven. The gauge set is modelled on Freidel–Louapre's gauge fixing (Section III), with spin 0 on a tree; there is no dual tree. Barrett–Naish-Guzman is cited for the cutoff and the Pachner moves only; they do not read the cutoff as a gauge fixing.
- **LL-0029.** Combinatorial 3-manifold in the sense of Lickorish's Definition 2.2 (every vertex link a combinatorial 2-sphere, for closed complexes). Pachner's theorem (Lickorish's Theorem 5.9) motivates the moves; it is not what is proved here.
- **LL-0030.** The statement `PR.PonzanoReggeFormula` (PonzanoRegge/Asymptotics.lean) is proved without hypotheses by `ponzanoReggeFormula`, through the large-spin asymptotics of the Racah sum (`racahSumAsymptotics`), and checked numerically. It is the Ponzano–Regge form, with edge lengths j + 1/2 in the volume and the angles. That form is equivalent to Roberts' Theorem 1, which uses the unshifted tetrahedron, via his Section 6.1 (Schläfli identity).

| LL-XXXX-a | There is no drawing of the complete bipartite graph K₃,₃ in the plane by continuous arcs (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PL.ContDrawing`, `Lightlike.PL.no_K33` in [ContK33.lean](../Lightlike/PL/ContK33.lean) |
| LL-XXXX-b | The weak Jordan theorem: the complement of a circle embedded in the plane is not connected (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PL.weak_jordan` in [WeakJordanCircle.lean](../Lightlike/PL/WeakJordanCircle.lean) |
| LL-XXXX-c | A Jordan curve is approximated by simple polygons, within any distance in both directions (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PL.exists_polygon_near`, `Lightlike.PL.exists_two_chains` in [PolygonApprox.lean](../Lightlike/PL/PolygonApprox.lean) |
| LL-XXXX-d | The complement of a Jordan curve has exactly one unbounded component and a bounded component whose frontier lies in the curve (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PL.jordan_components` in [JordanComponents.lean](../Lightlike/PL/JordanComponents.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-0064.** Two simplicial complexes whose geometric realisations are PL homeomorphic (a map piecewise linear on one realisation and bijective onto the other) are related by finitely many stellar moves (StellarEquiv.of_plHomeomorphic). The proof shows that every geometric subdivision is stellar equivalent to the complex it subdivides (subdivStellar, Lightlike/PL/SubdivCells.lean), by induction on the dimension: a subdivision is cut out by finitely many affine functionals, the slicings of the two complexes are isomorphic (stellarEquiv_of_cutting), and each complex is stellar equivalent to its slicing. Both complexes must have or both lack the empty face: the complex with no faces is a geometric subdivision of {∅}, both with empty underlying set, but the two are not stellar equivalent (not_stellarEquiv_void_null).
- **LL-0065.** For a closed combinatorial n-manifold K and a complex L, both containing the empty face, K and L are PL homeomorphic exactly when they are related by finitely many bistellar moves (pachner_plHomeomorphic). It combines Newman's theorem (LL-0064), which turns a PL homeomorphism into stellar equivalence, with the stellar version of Pachner's theorem (LL-0023), which turns stellar equivalence of a closed combinatorial manifold into bistellar equivalence; conversely, bistellar equivalence gives stellar equivalence (LL-0023), and stellar equivalent complexes are PL homeomorphic (PLHomeomorphic.of_stellarEquiv). The hypothesis is Lickorish's combinatorial manifold: isClosedCombManifold_iff_plHomeomorphic shows that the vertex links being stellar equivalent to boundaries of simplices (the definition used here) is the same as their being PL homeomorphic to them (Lickorish, Definition 2.2), by Newman's theorem (LL-0064) and PLHomeomorphic.of_stellarEquivIn. Check: the boundary of a triangle and its subdivision at a new vertex on an edge are related by bistellar moves, derived through the PL homeomorphism of a stellar subdivision (PLHomeomorphic.starAt).
- **LL-0076.** The complement of a simple closed polygon in the plane is the disjoint union of two nonempty, open, connected sets, one bounded (the inside) and one unbounded (the outside), and the polygon is the frontier of each (polygon_jordan, frontier_class). The proof uses the parity of the number of edges met by the horizontal ray to the right of a point, with a half-open rule at the endpoints. A bounded or unbounded connected piece of any such decomposition is identified with the inside or outside (eq_inside_of_isBounded), and the inside of a simple triangle is the interior of its convex hull (inside_eq_interior_hull). Simplicity (nondegenerate edges, non-consecutive edges disjoint, consecutive edges meeting only at the shared vertex) is needed: the bow tie has crossing edges (not_isSimple_bowtie). Checks: the triangle (0,0),(1,0),(0,1) is simple (triangle_isSimple), a polygon with a repeated vertex is not (not_isSimple_degenerate).
- **LL-0082.** A simple closed polygon with n ≥ 3 vertices has a triangulation: a finite family of triangles, each spanned by three vertices of the polygon, whose faces form a geometric complex (IsGeom) whose underlying set is the closed region bounded by the polygon (the inside together with the carrier), and in which every edge of the polygon is a face (exists_triangulation). The proof is by induction on n. A triangle is its own triangulation (isTriangulation_triangle). A polygon with at least four vertices has an interior diagonal, a pair of non-neighbouring vertices whose open segment lies in the inside: the extreme vertex has no vertex strictly inside its wedge below the nearest vertex of its corner triangle, or else the two neighbours of the extreme vertex span the diagonal. The diagonal splits the polygon into two simple polygons whose insides are disjoint and add up, with the open diagonal, to the inside (Polygon.inside_split), and the two triangulations fit together along the diagonal (isTriangulation_union). Limits: this entry does not say that the complex is a PL ball (that is the next entry); the triangles use only the polygon's own vertices; the polygon is simple in the sense of Polygon.IsSimple (no repeated vertices, non-consecutive edges disjoint). Check: the theorem applies to the triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) (triangle_triangulation, whose hypothesis is the simplicity checked in triangle_isSimple); the bow tie, which is not simple, is excluded (not_isSimple_bowtie).
- **LL-0083.** A simple closed polygon with n ≥ 3 vertices has a triangulation by its own vertices (see the previous entry), in which every edge of the polygon lies in exactly one triangle (EdgeUnique), and the complex generated by the triangles is a PL ball in the sense of the library, stellar equivalent to a simplex (IsBallIn; exists_ball_triangulation). The proof is by induction on n by clipping an ear: a simple polygon with at least four vertices has an interior diagonal between the vertices k and k + 2 (an ear), found by induction from the splitting along an interior diagonal (Polygon.two_ears: of two ears with non-neighbouring indices in a part, at most one touches the diagonal). The ear triangle is attached to the triangulation of the polygon with the ear removed along the diagonal, which lies in exactly one triangle there; attaching a triangle on a new vertex along such a boundary edge is a stellar equivalence, a stellar subdivision of the edge followed by a bistellar flip (SComplex.stellarEquivIn_closure_insert), so the complex stays a PL ball (ball_step). Limits: this entry does not identify the boundary of the ball with the polygon (the next entry does); the ball is combinatorial (IsBallIn, stellar equivalent to a simplex) with a geometric realisation given by the triangles, not shown here to be PL homeomorphic to a triangle. The polygon is simple in the sense of Polygon.IsSimple. Check: the theorem applies to the triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) (triangle_ball).
- **LL-0084.** For a simple closed polygon p with n ≥ 3 vertices there is a geometric complex K in the plane (IsGeom) whose underlying set is the closed region bounded by p (the inside together with the carrier), which is a PL ball (IsBallIn, stellar equivalent to a simplex), and whose boundary complex (SComplex.bd: the faces inside a face whose link is a PL ball) has underlying set exactly the polygon (polygon_schoenflies). The complex is the ear-clipping triangulation of the previous entry. The new ingredients are the invariant that every edge of the triangulation that is not an edge of the polygon lies in two triangles (NonBdry), and the computation, by the signed count of the link, that a face whose link is a ball lies in exactly one triangle (unique_triangle_of_ball); the faces of the boundary are then exactly the faces inside an edge of the polygon (mem_bd_closure_iff), and their hulls are the edges (bd_space_eq_carrier). Limits: the ball is combinatorial (stellar equivalent to a simplex) with the geometric realisation given by the triangles; a PL homeomorphism of the region onto a triangle is not constructed, and this is the polygonal case only, not the Schoenflies theorem for arbitrary Jordan curves. The polygon is simple in the sense of Polygon.IsSimple. Check: the theorem applies to the triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) (triangle_schoenflies); the bow tie, which is not simple, is excluded (not_isSimple_bowtie).
- **LL-0090.** For a simple closed polygon p with n ≥ 3 vertices there is a geometric complex K in the plane whose underlying set is the closed region bounded by p (the inside together with the carrier), and a map f with IsPLHomeo K (simplex {(0,0), (1,0), (0,1)}) f, a PL homeomorphism of the region onto the standard triangle (polygon_plHomeo_triangle). The complex is the ear-clipping triangulation, which is a PL ball (stellar equivalent to a simplex). Stellar equivalent complexes are PL homeomorphic for the canonical realisations (the easy half of Lickorish, Theorem 4.5, PLHomeomorphic.of_stellarEquivIn); a geometric complex is PL homeomorphic to its canonical realisation by the linear map x ↦ ∑ x v • v (SComplex.isPLHomeo_real_geom, using that the faces are affinely independent and meet in common faces, Lickorish Definition 2.1); and a ball of dimension n is PL homeomorphic to the simplex on any n + 1 vertices (SComplex.PLHomeomorphic.of_isPLBallIn). Limits: the homeomorphism is not shown to map the polygon onto the boundary of the triangle (boundary invariance of PL homeomorphisms is not proved in the library); this is the polygonal case only, not the Schoenflies theorem for arbitrary Jordan curves. The polygon is simple in the sense of Polygon.IsSimple. Check: the theorem applies to the triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) (triangle_plHomeo); the bow tie, which is not simple, is excluded (not_isSimple_bowtie).
- **LL-0091.** Six distinct points u i, v j (i, j ∈ Fin 3) joined across the two classes by nine simple polygonal arcs (finite chains of segments, IsSimpleChain) that meet only in common endpoints do not exist (no_PL_K33; PLDrawing is the notion of drawing, for a set E of edges). This is the second claim of the proof of the weak Jordan theorem by Thomassen in the exposition of Klazar, Section 2, Claim 2 (Klazar's numbering), restricted to polygonal arcs. The proof differs from the orientation (left/right) argument there: the 6-cycle u0 v0 u1 v1 u2 v2 is a simple polygon (two arcs glued by isSimpleChain_append), and each of the three remaining arcs is a chord joining opposite corners. Each chord, without its ends, lies in the inside or in the outside of the polygon (it is connected and misses the carrier). Two of the three chords lie on the same side, and two chords on the same side cannot join interlaced pairs of the polygon's points (no_interlaced_chord): the proof uses only that the crossing parity of a ray, which is a count modulo 2, is additive when a closed chain is cut along a chord and glued from the two halves (chainParity_append, chainParity_reverse, parity_theta), and that the parity jumps across an arc near its interior points (near_two). A rotation of the labels does not change the inside and outside of the hexagon (inside_swap), so the same lemma covers every pair of chords (Hex.false). Limits: the arcs are polygonal arcs only; the statement for arbitrary continuous arcs is Klazar, Claim 3, a later step, and is not claimed here. Check: the drawing of K₃,₃ without the edge (2, 2), with straight segments, exists (TestsK33.drawing, so the hypotheses are satisfiable); two crossing diagonals of a square violate the disjointness field.
- **LL-XXXX-a.** Six distinct points u i, v j (i, j ∈ Fin 3) joined across the two classes by nine continuous injective arcs γ i j : [0, 1] → ℝ² from u i to v j that meet only in common endpoints do not exist (no_K33; ContDrawing is the notion of drawing). This is Claim 3 of the proof of the weak Jordan theorem by Thomassen in the exposition of Klazar, Section 2 (Klazar's numbering). The polygonal case is LL-0091. The reduction to it follows Klazar: radius r such that the closed balls around the six points are disjoint and an arc keeps distance larger than r from the points that are not its ends; each arc is trimmed to the subarc between the last visit of the ball around its first end and the first visit of the ball around its second end (exists_trim); a polygonal chain within ε of the trimmed subarc is obtained from the values of the arc at the points k/N, which gives a chain by uniform continuity (exists_chain_near), and loop erasure turns it into a simple chain in the same set (exists_simple_sub); with ε smaller than a third of the distance between any two trimmed subarcs, the chains are pairwise disjoint and meet the segments from the vertices to the ends of the trimmed subarcs only at the ends of those segments (the segment argument uses that two segments from a centre to different points of one sphere meet only at the centre, segment_inter_sphere); the nine chains, loop-erased with the segments, form a polygonal drawing of K₃,₃, which does not exist by LL-0091. Limits: the arcs are injective continuous images of [0, 1] in the plane; the statement is for K₃,₃ only and does not say anything about the Jordan curve theorem by itself (the next entry). Check: the straight-line drawing of K₃,₃ without the edge (2, 2) of LL-0091 is a drawing by continuous arcs (TestsJordan.contDrawing, ContDrawingOn), so the hypotheses are satisfiable.
- **LL-XXXX-b.** For a continuous injective map f of the circle into the plane, the complement of the image is not connected (weak_jordan). This is Claim 4 of the proof of the weak Jordan theorem by Thomassen in the exposition of Klazar, Section 2 (Klazar's numbering). The proof: if the image is not contained in a horizontal line, take a highest point a and a lowest point b of the image; rotating the circle, the image is the union of two arcs from a to b that meet only at a and b (exists_two_arcs); if the complement were connected, an outer polygonal arc from a to b is drawn around the image (exists_outer), a horizontal segment between a point c of the first arc and a point d of the second is chosen at minimal distance so that its interior misses both arcs (exists_T), and an arc from an interior point e of the segment to a point g of the outer arc is drawn in the complement (exists_link, using polygonal connectedness of connected open sets, exists_chain_in_open); the nine arcs between a, b, e and c, d, g that this cuts out of the pieces have mutually disjoint interiors (false_of_pieces), a drawing of K₃,₃ by continuous arcs, which does not exist by LL-XXXX-a. If the image lies in a horizontal line the coordinates are swapped. Limits: this is the weak Jordan theorem only: the complement is not connected, but it is not shown to have exactly two components, one bounded and one unbounded, with the circle as the boundary of each; this needs the arc theorem (the complement of an arc is connected), which is not proved here. Check: the unit circle satisfies the hypotheses (TestsJordan, unitCircle), and a non-injective map does not.
- **LL-XXXX-c.** For a continuous injective map f of the circle into the plane and ε > 0 there is a list of points whose polygon is simple, such that every point of its carrier is within ε of the image of f and every point of the image is within ε of the carrier (exists_polygon_near; the Hausdorff distance between the carrier and the curve is less than ε). The circle is cut into two arcs from a = f 1 to b = f (-1) that meet only at a and b (exists_two_arcs); each arc is trimmed outside small balls around a and b (exists_trim), approximated by a simple chain near the trimmed subarc (exists_simple_chain_near, with loop erasure), and joined to the vertices by segments; the two resulting chains meet only at a and b, by the three arguments of no_K33 specialised to two arcs (exists_two_chains), and glue to a simple polygon (isSimple_two_arcs). The loop erasure could delete a loop of the sample chain and leave part of the arc far from the polygon; this does not happen because the inverse of an arc is uniformly continuous, so that a connected compact set that contains both ends of the arc and lies near it is near every point of it (arc_density, exists_inverse_modulus; Lightlike/PL/ArcDensity.lean). Limits: it approximates by a simple closed polygon, but says nothing about on which side of the polygon the curve lies; that the curve separates the plane into exactly two components needs the Arc Theorem and is not proved here. Check: the theorem applies to the unit circle (TestsJordan.unitCircle); two arcs that cross in a point of their interiors would not have simple chains meeting only at their ends, and the hypothesis of exists_two_chains excludes them.
- **LL-XXXX-d.** For a continuous injective map f of the circle into the plane, the complement of the image has exactly one unbounded connected component (the one that contains the plane outside a square around the curve, which is connected, isPreconnected_squareOutside), and, since the complement is not connected (weak_jordan, LL-XXXX-b), a bounded component whose frontier lies in the curve (jordan_components). Limits: this is the part of the Jordan curve theorem that holds without the Arc Theorem. That there is exactly one bounded component, and that the curve is the frontier of each component, are open here: they need the Arc Theorem (the complement of an arc is connected), for which no proof is available in this library, and are not claimed. Check: the unit circle satisfies the hypotheses (TestsJordan.unitCircle).

Notes:

- **LL-0070.** For the finite q-Racah sum SR at q = e^{iπ/r}, the three-term recurrence in the third colour holds under explicit conditions: some a_i = L + 1 with L ≥ 0, b₁ - a_i ≤ r - 2, b₂ - L ≤ r - 2, b₃ - L ≤ r - 2, and r does not divide b₂ + b₃ - a₂ - a₃ + k for k = 0, 1, 2. The case where all a_i = 0, and the case where r divides one of those quantum-integer arguments (which occurs for admissible data), are not covered by this statement. Compare Koekoek–Swarttouw (3.2.5); the coefficients were not compared term by term with that source.
- **LL-0071.** The row identity for qSixJ in the third colour, for all admissible data, the two endpoint colours 0 and r - 2 included (row_at, which packages sixj_row for the interior colours with the separate proofs of the two endpoint rows). r ≥ 3 is needed at the top endpoint. Not shown: the recurrence in the other colours.
- **LL-0072.** The weights jOmega make the recurrence coefficients symmetric (detailed balance, sixj_balance); an abstract weighted Jacobi lemma (jacobi_orth) then gives orthogonality of the q-6j sums for different sixth colours (sixj_offdiag; by duality also in the sixth colour, sixj_offdiag_dual). It uses that the eigenvalues 2 cos((q+1)π/r) are distinct. Not shown: the value of the diagonal norm.
- **LL-0073.** The weighted norms of all rows and all columns of the matrix of q-6j sums are one common constant (Gram-matrix argument, gram_const for the columns and sixj_norm_const for the rows). Its value is not proved by these results; see the two conditional results that follow.
- **LL-0074.** Under the boundary evaluation QDougall (the terminating very-well-poised 6φ5 summation at the lowest sixth colour, the q-Dougall summation), every weighted norm equals 1. QDougall is an explicit hypothesis, not proved in Lean in general. It is satisfiable: the instance at level r = 2 (qDougall_two, where the only colour is 0) is proved, and another at level r = 3 (qDougall_three); this says nothing about larger r, where it is checked numerically (exact at r = 4 to 7).
- **LL-0075.** Given QDougallAll (the q-Dougall boundary evaluation for all admissible colours), the diagonal orthogonality qOrthogonality of the model holds at every level r ≥ 2. Together with qBiedenharnElliott this would give the Turaev–Viro invariance of LL-0031 at level r. Not proved: QDougallAll itself, and qBiedenharnElliott for r ≥ 4. The hypothesis is satisfiable at level r = 2 (qDougallAll_two, where the only colour is 0); this says nothing about r ≥ 3, where QDougall is checked numerically (exact at r = 4 to 7).

- **LL-0047.** Both propositions are proved (coh15jAsymptoticFormula in MaxSetFinite.lean, eprlAsymptoticFormula in EPRLFormula.lean). For a nondegenerate 4-simplex, spins proportional to its triangle areas with an even spin sum at every node, and a nonsingular Hessian at both critical points, the coherent 15j integral over SU(2)^5 in the Regge boundary state is (2π/λ)^6 2^4 (4π)^-8 (e^(iλS) A₊ + e^(-iλS) A₋) + O(λ^-7), with S the Regge action Σ (n_e/2) Θ_e (Coh15jAsymptoticFormula). The EPRL form, for 0 < γ < 1, has four terms with phases ±S and ±γS and remainder O(λ^-13) (EPRLAsymptoticFormula); it follows from two instances of the 15j form by Fubini, as in Barrett–Fairbairn–Hellmann. BFH's sign factor (−1)^χ is not part of the statement. Equality of the coherent integral with eprlVertex on Livine–Speziale intertwiners is not proven, and the nonsingular Hessian is a hypothesis, as in Barrett et al. At the regular 4-simplex every hypothesis except the Hessian conditions is checked in the kernel (regular_coh15j_hyps, regular_eprl_hyps); the Hessian conditions are checked numerically (Re(−H) positive definite, det(−H₊) ≈ 1185 − 898i for doubled spins 3). Spins not proportional to the areas, or with an odd node sum, violate them (regular_wrong_spins); boundary data that do not glue are exponentially suppressed (coh15j_exp_decay, coh15j_oneData_decay). Checked numerically against the exact integral at the regular 4-simplex (scripts/asymptotics/eprl_asymptotics_check.py).

NOT PROVED: that hessBlockMatrix is the matrix of second derivatives of the action in a chart at a critical point (needs the chart and the vanishing of the first derivative), and the nondegeneracy of the matrix (BDFHP eq. (57) assumes it without proof, Sec. 6.4, p. 30).
- **LL-0098.** At a critical configuration (IsLorCritical, critical spinors), with p = gamma k, unit boundary spinors, closure at the node, and the overlap products off the cut of the logarithm, the second derivative of lorAction along X_a Y(t) for a curve Y with Y(0) = 1 and Y' = Y genMat(cv(t)), cv differentiable at 0, equals the sum of the end formulas of hessXX_block at the velocity cv(0): the derivative cv'(0) contributes the first variation in the direction genMat(cv'(0)), which is zero by closure (srcCoeff_adj_gen, tgtCoeff_adj_gen identify it with the logarithmic derivative). hessXX_block is the case of a constant velocity. This is the independence of the Hessian of the curve at a critical point for the node variables. NOT PROVED: the same for the spinor variables and the mixed block (hessZZ_block and hessXZ_block do not need criticality and are stated for straight lines in z), and the identification of the matrix of second derivatives in a chart with hessBlockMatrix (needs the chart and the congruence by its differential).

Notes:

- **LL-0048.** Sorkin's complex Lorentzian angles, with the complex action weighted by Z = -i on spacelike and 1 on timelike triangles. For a 4D triangulation embedded in Minkowski space, every deficit angle vanishes (IsGeometric4.lorDeficit_eq_zero), the action is differentiable in the squared edge lengths with the Lorentzian Schläfli identity (lorSchlaefli4_finset, hasFDerivAt_lorReggeAction), and the flat configuration is stationary (lorReggeAction_stationary). Euclidean angles on the same Lorentzian data give deficit π, so the Lorentzian angles are needed (wrong_eucAngle_T). Null triangles and tetrahedra are excluded (IsNonNull4); the null cases are not covered. Checked numerically (scripts/regge).
- **LL-0053.** For a Riemannian metric on a region of the plane, ρ-fat vertex stars of bounded valence with geodesic edge lengths and mesh h, and a Lipschitz weight f, |Σ_v f(v) δ_v − ∫ f K dA| ≤ C h. The angle bound of the stars is derived from fatness (Lightlike.CMS.angle_le_of_fat). The vertex cells, of area ½Σ det2 and covering the region three times outside a boundary layer of area at most b h, are hypotheses; building them from an explicit triangulation is not proven, so this is not yet the theorem of Cheeger, Müller and Schrader (Commun. Math. Phys. 92 (1984) 405), which is in every dimension. As checks, the flat metric gives density 0, the round sphere gives 4π, and the curvature density without the area weight gives 2π², not 4π. Non-vacuity is shown on a single flat star with four neighbours, which meets every hypothesis with an empty region Ω (the cell is its own boundary layer); a non-empty region is LL-0054's grid.
- **LL-0054.** The vertex cells of LL-0053 are built from a triangulation given by vertex positions and corner maps, not assumed. The star cell of an interior vertex is the union of its triangles, its area is ½Σ det2, and the triangles cover the interior region three times outside the triangles with a corner off V. The corners of a star triangle agree with (v, nb v j, nb v (j+1)) up to a permutation of Fin 3; the first version of the statement fixed their order, which left no triangle with all corners in V, and was corrected. The remaining hypotheses are that distinct triangles overlap in null sets, that the star of every interior vertex winds once (its angles sum to 2π), that the number of boundary triangles times h is bounded, that every triangle lies in K, and that edges at the first corner of each triangle have length at most h; the integral runs over the triangles with all three corners in V. Non-vacuity is shown on a 4×4 vertex grid with the 4 central vertices interior, valence 6 and the flat metric (Lightlike.CMS.grid_triangulation_bound), with 2 interior and 16 boundary triangles and an interior region of positive area (Lightlike.CMS.grid_interior_positive); the flat metric makes the integral 0. For a non-flat metric the n×n grids of the unit square, h = 1/n, satisfy the hypotheses with constants independent of n, so the deficit sum is within C/n of the interior integral for every large n (Lightlike.CMS.refining_grid_bound); for the metric dx² + e^{2x}dy² of scalar curvature −2 (Lightlike.CMS.scalar_hyp) that integral is at most −1/4 for every n ≥ 4 (Lightlike.CMS.hyp_refining_grid). The deficit angles there are those of the chart geodesic distances, which are not computed explicitly. As wrong-model checks, a clockwise star fails the fatness hypothesis for every ρ > 0 (Lightlike.CMS.reversed_star_not_fat), and Lightlike.CMS.volume_real_tri_example computes a triangle area of 3, not the 6 of the unhalved determinant. This is the planar case only, not the theorem of Cheeger, Müller and Schrader in every dimension.
- **LL-0056.** For a Riemannian coordinate metric g on U and a compact K ⊆ U, |d(m − Δ/2, m + Δ/2)² − g_m(Δ,Δ) − Q_m(Δ)| ≤ C‖Δ‖⁶ for m in K and small Δ, with the quartic form Q_m(Δ) = (1/24)∂_Δ∂_Δ g(Δ,Δ) − (1/12)g(Γ(Δ,Δ),Γ(Δ,Δ)); about the midpoint the terms of order three and five vanish. The order is sharp: on the cubic shear the remainder is t⁶/576 along Δ = (t, 0), so it is not O(‖Δ‖⁷) (Lightlike.Geodesic.dist_sq_expansion_midpoint6_sharp), and the expansion is checked exactly there (Lightlike.Geodesic.cubicShear_dist_sq_expansion_midpoint6). Brewin (2009), Section 9, gives the expansion in Riemann normal coordinates and the midpoint form d² = g(m)(Δ, Δ) + O(‖Δ‖⁴); the quartic form Q_m and the sixth-order bound are derived here.
- **LL-0057.** For the Riemannian bundle of g on U, Mathlib's riemannianEDist is the infimum of the lengths of admissible curves, with no hypothesis on the points (the empty infimum is ⊤). If an admissible curve joins x and y it equals ENNReal.ofReal (dist g U x y), and on a preconnected U this holds for all x, y. Without an admissible curve riemannianEDist is ⊤ while the chart distance takes the junk value 0. This connects the geodesic results of this library (LL-0045, LL-0056) to Mathlib's Riemannian distance.
- **LL-0058.** The map from the ten squared edge lengths of a 4-simplex to its ten squared triangle areas (Heron's formula in squared lengths) has invertible Jacobian at the regular simplex (all squared lengths 1; jac_regular_isUnit, through an explicit integer inverse of the edge-triangle incidence matrix), so by the inverse function theorem it is injective on a neighbourhood of the regular simplex with open image, and so are the areas themselves. The result is local: at the corner configuration (squared lengths 1 on the edges at one vertex, 2 on the others) the Jacobian is singular (jac_corner_det, with an explicit kernel vector), and corner_pair gives two different length assignments, the corner configuration moved by plus and minus half that kernel vector, both satisfying the Gram-minor criterion IsSimplex, with the same ten areas. IsSimplex is the positivity of the leading principal minors of the Gram matrix; Realization.lean gives both assignments as the squared distances of affinely independent five-point sets in ℝ⁴, so they are Euclidean 4-simplices of non-zero volume (Lightlike.AreaRegge.corner_pair_realized). scripts/regge/area_jacobian_check.py recomputes det Jac = −48/8¹⁰ at the regular simplex, the corner kernel and the corner pair in SymPy.
- **LL-0063.** For a symmetric, C³, compactly supported perturbation h of the flat metric of the plane and a C¹ compactly supported weight f, the weighted sum of the linearized vertex deficit angles of the diagonal grid of mesh 1/n differs from ∫ f · linCurv h by at most C/n, where linCurv h = ∂₀∂₁h₀₁ − ½(∂₁²h₀₀ + ∂₀²h₁₁) is the linearized Gauss curvature (linearized_regge_converges). The squared edge lengths are ∫₀¹ (δ + εh)(e, e) dt along the edge vector e, that is ℓ_e²(1 + ε ⨍_e h(t_e, t_e)), Christiansen's degrees of freedom of the Regge interpolant (eq. (5)); this is the first variation of the squared length, not the distance of the perturbed metric; tying them to that distance is open. For a quadratic perturbation the deficit is exactly s² linCurv (linDef_model), and the flat star has deficit 0. Christiansen works in dimension 3; this is the 2D analogue on one grid family, and the Regge action itself is not treated. A perturbation with a positive limit shows non-vacuity, and dropping the ∂₀∂₁h₀₁ term gives the limit 0, which the deficits do not approach. The nonlinear 2D statement, for geodesic edge lengths, is LL-0053 (after Cheeger, Müller and Schrader).
- **LL-0078.** G is any positive definite 3x3 matrix; the incidences are the 36 pairs (tetrahedron, hinge) of the Kuhn triangulation of the unit cube (six tetrahedra, seven edge directions). Each class of incidences is a fan of four or six tetrahedra around the hinge axis; the proof uses the complex coordinate in the plane quotient, so it holds for every G and does not use G = identity. Limits: only the cube star of one lattice point is treated; nothing is said about a triangulation of a manifold, and the lattice is the standard one (no other triangulations).
- **LL-0079.** For a coordinate metric g on an open set U (smooth, symmetric, invertible) and a point m of U: the derivative of the inverse metric is minus g⁻¹ (∂g) g⁻¹ (pd_inv), and the derivative of the Christoffel symbols, the Riemann tensor and the scalar curvature at m are written with (g m)⁻¹, ∂g(m) and ∂∂g(m) only. Limits: this unfolds the coordinate definitions of the library (Lightlike.christoffel, riemann, scalarCurvature); it is the textbook computation, not a statement about tensors or charts.
- **LL-0080.** Part of the 3D convergence of the Regge action (T-RC6), which stays open. Scope: at a point m where all first partial derivatives of a Riemannian metric g on an open set of R^3 vanish (for example the centre of normal coordinates); not the general chart. The convergence theorem needs the same statement at every hinge, where the first derivatives do not vanish, and that case is open. For any positive definite g(m) and any second derivatives, the star of one edge of the Kuhn triangulation (flat star: the dihedral angles of each of the seven edge classes add up to 2π; first-order coefficient 0; weights: the hinge lengths √(g(m)(w, w)) of the seven directions w, where g(m)(w, w) is the squared length) satisfies: the sum over the seven classes of the hinge length times the second-order coefficient of the class angle sum equals minus half the scalar curvature times the square root of det g(m) (JetStarCore). The core is an exact polynomial identity in the six entries of g(m) and the 36 independent second derivatives (flat_star_identity), generated and checked in exact arithmetic by scripts/regge/gen_flat_star.py. Limits: second derivatives are those of g at the single point m; the Kuhn triangulation is the standard cubical one; the Gram lengths g(m) are the metric at m, not integrated along edges. Trust checks: the Euclidean metric satisfies the hypotheses, and for sphere-like second derivatives the sum over the 36 incidences is 3, not 0 and not 6 (FlatStarTests.lean).
- **LL-0092.** Part of the 3D convergence of the Regge action (T-RC6), which stays open. For a Riemannian metric g on U and m in U, displace every point k of the star around an edge to k + (ε/2) Γ(k, k) (Γ the Christoffel symbols at m). In each edge class the displaced tetrahedra form a closed fan around the displaced hinge axis that is positively oriented at ε = 0, so the sum of their dihedral angles (computed with the quadratic form g(m)) is 2π for all ε in a neighbourhood of 0 (a neighbourhood, no explicit radius). Uses closed fans of complex numbers, continuity in ε and the lattice result of LL-0078. Limits: one edge star of the standard cubical Kuhn triangulation, one point m; nothing about a triangulation of a manifold or about convergence.
- **LL-0093.** Part of the 3D convergence of the Regge action (T-RC6), which stays open: this is the jet-level statement at one point, not the convergence. For a Riemannian metric g on an open set U of R^3 and any point m of U (no condition on the first derivatives of g), the star of one edge of the standard Kuhn triangulation satisfies JetStarCore: admissible Gram lengths, angle sums 2π in the seven classes, vanishing first-order coefficient, and the sum over the classes of the hinge length (√(g(m)(w, w))) times the second-order coefficient equals minus half the scalar curvature times √det g(m). Proof: the edge polynomial of the jet of g equals that of a flat jet with second derivatives Sdd = ∂∂g - g ΓΓ after displacing the vertices by εΓ(k, k)/2 (edgeC_eq_chr, edgeR_eq_displaced), the displaced flat star has angle sums 2π (LL-0092) so its first- and second-order coefficients vanish (disp_coeffs), the flat identity of LL-0080 applies to Sdd, and the scalar curvature at m is that of the flat jet with Sdd (scalar_eq_flat; the transformation of the curvature under the change of chart is the tensor transformation law cited). Limits: second derivatives at the single point m; standard cubical Kuhn triangulation; no convergence statement, no manifold triangulation; Riemannian (positive definite) signature only. Trust checks: the Euclidean metric and diag(exp x0, 1, 1), whose first derivative at 0 is nonzero so that LL-0080 does not apply to it (ChartChangeTests.lean).

Notes:

- **LL-0049.** An identity at finite cutoff: the cutoff conditions make the cutoffs on the faces inside the move non-binding. The gauge rule (IsGauge: the vertices, the edges and the gauge triangles form a collapsible 2-complex) is this library's proposal for the 4D analogue of the maximal tree, not a construction from the literature. Non-vacuity: amplitudeGF_move33_example and amplitudeGF_move33_star1 check every hypothesis in the kernel on closed 4-spheres. A perturbed vertex amplitude breaks the identity (ampBad_breaks_move33). Removal of the cutoff and independence of the gauge set are not proven.
- **LL-0050.** An identity at finite cutoff: the cutoff conditions make the cutoffs on the faces inside the move non-binding. The 2-4 move adds one triangle to the gauge set (IsGauge.move24); the 4-2 move is the 2-4 move read backwards (the gauge set is given on the complex after the 4-2 move). Non-vacuity: amplitudeGF_move24_example checks every hypothesis of amplitudeGF_move24 in the kernel on the 1-5 subdivision of the boundary of the 5-simplex, with no gauge triangles, and amplitudeGF_move24_gauge_example does the same for the gauge-fixed form with a gauge set of fourteen triangles (isGauge_T14), so the gauge-fixed statement is instantiated in the kernel; the two sums are shown equal, their value is not computed. There is no wrong-model check for this move; the perturbed amplitude ampBad is checked against the 3-3 move only (LL-0049). Removal of the cutoff and independence of the gauge set are not proven.
- **LL-0051.** An identity at finite cutoff (the cutoff conditions Cut15 make the cutoffs on the faces inside the move non-binding). The 1-5 move adds the four triangles {v, a_0, a_j} to the gauge set (isGauge_move15); the 5-1 move is the 1-5 move read backwards (the gauge set is given on the complex after the 5-1 move). Non-vacuity: amplitudeGF_move15_example checks every hypothesis of amplitudeGF_move15 in the kernel on the boundary of the 5-simplex, with no gauge triangles, and amplitudeGF_move15_gauge_example does the same for the gauge-fixed form with the ten gauge triangles through a vertex (isGauge_starK0), so the gauge-fixed statement is instantiated in the kernel; the two sums are shown equal, their value is not computed. There is no wrong-model check for this move; the perturbed amplitude ampBad is checked against the 3-3 move only (LL-0049). Removal of the cutoff and independence of the gauge set are not proven.
- **LL-0052.** The vertex is the contraction along the edges of K₅ of five Barrett–Crane intertwiners Σ_i ι_i ⊗ ι_i, in the orthonormal intertwiner basis, with no dimension factor per tetrahedron and edge amplitude 1 (a normalisation convention). Baez and Christensen's Riemannian 10j symbol, when nonzero, is negative exactly when the ten spins sum to a half-integer; the vertex here is non-negative for all spins, so the two conventions differ by a sign. bcVertexBC, the vertex times (−1) to the sum of the doubled spins, follows their sign rule; its absolute value is the vertex, and it is ≥ 0 for even and ≤ 0 for odd sums (abs_bcVertexBC, bcVertexBC_nonneg_of_even, bcVertexBC_nonpos_of_odd). The sign rule is taken from Baez and Christensen; that bcVertexBC equals their 10j as they define it is not proven. On the triangle of spin j/2 the 15j symbol is 1/√(j + 1) and the vertex 1/(j + 1), so at spin 1/2 the two conventions give −1/2 and +1/2. Non-vacuity is shown by the value 1 at spin 0 and 1/(j + 1)² on the closed loop of spin j/2. No published table of 10j values was found to compare against.
- **LL-0060.** The twisted cochain complex of a finite 2-complex with an edge connection g and a real representation has d1 ∘ d0 = 0 exactly when g is flat and the face boundaries are closed walks (d1_comp_d0, TwistedCohomology.lean); H² = C²/im d1 is trivial iff d1 is onto (d1_surjective_iff). For SU(2) acting on su(2) = ℝ³ by the adjoint action, varying each edge holonomy along exp(tΦ_e)g_e changes the face holonomies at a flat connection with derivative d1 Φ (holonomy_hasDerivAt), so a first-order change X of the face holonomies is realised exactly when X = d1 Φ (face_variation_iff). The tests: d1 is onto for the disc and not onto for the 2-sphere with one edge, and a non-flat connection breaks d1 ∘ d0 = 0 (TwistedCohomologyTests.lean, real multiplicative coefficients). For SU(2) with the adjoint action, the 2-sphere with one edge and two faces at the trivial connection has d1 not onto and H² ≠ 0 (sphere_su2_H2_nontrivial, TwistedCohomologyTests.lean); on the disc at the trivial connection d1 is onto and every face-holonomy variation is realised (disc_su2_d1_surjective, disc_su2_face_variation), so both sides of the criterion are instantiated for SU(2). Barrett and Naish-Guzman's theorem (§4.4) is existence of the partition function as a distribution; only the finite-dimensional step, d1 = the differential of the holonomy map, is proved here, not the measure-theoretic step. Not covered: the link from H² = 0 to the removal of the Ponzano–Regge cut-off.
- **LL-0061.** The sum rule Σ_{a ≤ 2c} (−1)^a (2a+1) {a c c; c c c} = δ_{c0} follows from the orthogonality of the 6j symbols (racah_sum, from sixJSym_orth_all). For Bing's house with two rooms, BNG §2.4 write the Ponzano–Regge sum as Z = Σ_c Σ_{b ≤ 2c} Σ_{a ≤ 2c} (−1)^(a+b) (2a+1)(2b+1)(2c+1) {a c c; c c c}{b c c; c c c}. Its summand stays of order 1 at large spins, so the sum is not absolutely convergent and its value depends on how it is summed; the model takes its value from a regularisation. Two summations are proved here (Lean uses doubled spins). Room spins first: for each central spin c the sums over a and b run to their full range 2c, where each is δ_{c0}, and any cut-off N on c then gives 1 (bingIterated_eq_one). Simple cut-off Λ on all spins (BNG §2.2): at Λ = 1 the room sums for c = 1 stop at a = 1 instead of 2, which drops the term 5/6 (from {2 1 1; 1 1 1} = 1/6), so Z_1 = 1 + 3 (5/6)² = 37/12 (bingCutoff_two, bingCutoff_two_ne_iterated). 37/12 is one partial sum, not a limit: Z_Λ has no limit (BNG fig. 6, numerical; scripts/spinfoam/bing_house_check.py computes Z_Λ exactly up to Λ = 14, with values between 1 and 8.15 that do not settle). The two values therefore show no inconsistency of the Ponzano–Regge model: the simple cut-off truncates the room sums before 2c, which BNG give as the cause of its divergence, and BNG state (not proved here) that the Turaev–Viro regularisation gives 1 for every q. The sum formula is taken from BNG §2.4; it is not derived in Lean from a state sum on a 2-complex. Not covered: that H² = 0 makes the cut-off removable (BNG §4.4).
- **LL-0066.** For edge spins s (doubled units; edges 01, 02, 03, 12, 13, 23) the integral over SU(2)^4 of Π_e χ_{s e}(g_i g_j⁻¹) equals {s₀₁ s₀₂ s₀₃; s₂₃ s₁₃ s₁₂}² (tetraInt_eq_sixJ_sq). The proof expands each character in the matrix coefficients of the spin representations, integrates them with the Haar measure into products of 3j vectors, and identifies the resulting sum with a 6j symbol up to a sign (ZR_eq). This is Freidel–Louapre's Ponzano–Regge observable of the 1-skeleton of the two-tetrahedron triangulation of S³, eq. (94), read on the dual graph: their group variables sit on the four triangles and the holonomy around an edge is g_i g_j⁻¹ for the two triangles i, j containing it, so the Lean edge ij carries the spin of the edge shared by triangles i and j, and the triads at the Lean vertices are the triangles of the triangulation. Checks: all spins 0 give 1 (tetraInt_zero), all spins 1 (doubled spin 2) give (1/6)² = 1/36 (tetraInt_two), and an inadmissible triad at a vertex gives 0 (tetraInt_eq_zero_of_not_tri, tetraInt_ones_vertex).
- **LL-0067.** The tetrahedron sum over the six doubled edge spins up to a cut-off N has the nonnegative terms Π(s_e+1)·{s₀ s₁ s₂; s₅ s₄ s₃}² (tetraTerm_nonneg). At the doubled spins (0, n, n, n, n, 0) the dimension factor is (n+1)⁴ and the 6j symbol is ±1/(n+1) by the zero-spin formula (sixJSym_zero_left; DLMF eq. 34.5.1 after the 34.5(ii) column symmetry), so the term is (n+1)² (tetraTerm_zeroSpin). Hence the sum is at least (N+1)² (tetraPartition_ge), it is unbounded (tetraPartition_unbounded), and by the monotone-limit criterion it has no limit (not_tetraRemovable). This is the sum without the rescaling M_Λ^{-v} of the simple cut-off of Barrett and Naish-Guzman (§2.2), who do not define M_Λ here; whether the rescaled limit exists is not decided. The tests: the cut-off values 1, 29, 2393/4 at doubled cut-offs 0, 1, 2 are numerical (scripts/spinfoam/tetra_partition_check.py) and lie above (N+1)². Not covered: existence of the sum as a distribution and H² = 0 (Barrett and Naish-Guzman, §4.4), and the link from H² = 0 to the removal of the cut-off.
- **LL-0068.** The three moves 3-3, 2-4 and 1-5 (LL-0049 to LL-0051) are put into one relation GFStep4 on triples (complex, gauge set, cutoffs), with the hypotheses of the three move theorems and a step recut that changes the cutoffs on faces that are not summed (amplitudeGF_congr_cut). A step takes a gauge set to a gauge set (GFStep4.isGauge), and the gauge-fixed amplitude is constant along every chain of steps and their inverses, which are the 4-2 and 5-1 moves (amplitudeGF_eqvGen4). If a gauge set T forces every triangle, the state sum is 1 at every constant cutoff, so it converges as the cutoff is removed (amplitudeGF_tendsto_one_of_forces). Non-vacuity: amplitudeGF_chain_example runs a 1-5 move followed by a 2-4 move on the boundary of the 5-simplex with ten gauge triangles; amplitudeGF_tendsto_starT is the forcing case on the boundary of the 5-simplex. The gauge rule is this library's proposal for the 4D analogue of the maximal tree of Freidel and Louapre (Section IV.B of the paper, the gauge-fixing procedure; the location checked in the registry is the title of Section IV), not a construction from the literature; their independence of the choice of tree is argued there by BRST invariance and is formal. Not proven: finite cutoff only, the cutoffs must be re-chosen by recut between moves and the cutoff conditions are sufficient, not necessary; independence of the gauge set is not proven for gauge sets that do not force every triangle (numerical examples in scripts/spinfoam/gauge_independence_check.py show finite-cutoff dependence for non-forcing sets); the second tree, the global symmetry left at the root vertex, the Faddeev-Popov measure and the limit of the ungauged sum are not treated. Observation, not a proof: for the gauge set of the closed 4-sphere with 24 4-simplices in scripts/spinfoam/gauge_manifold_check.py, which obeys the gauge rule but forces only 38 of its 62 triangles, the cutoff state sum at doubled cutoffs 2, 4, ..., 40 (scripts/spinfoam/gauge_cutoff_limit.py; exact 3j symbols, double-precision contraction, summation-order spread 3e-15 at cutoff 10 and 8e-14 at cutoff 20, not measured at larger cutoffs) changes sign seven times and its largest absolute value grows from 6.0 (cutoffs up to 8) to 33.8 (cutoffs from 12), so numerically the cutoff sums do not settle for that gauge set. The check at 32 and above in higher precision is open. On the boundary of the 5-simplex and on two small 4-spheres every sampled gauge set (3000, 2000 and 2000 random sets) forces every triangle.
- **LL-0069.** Forcing is the rule that a tetrahedron with three of its triangles in the set forces the fourth (Forces); the rule is this library's, used to show that the gauge-fixed state sum is 1 (amplitudeGF_tendsto_one_of_forces). Forces is monotone in the tetrahedra and in the starting set (Forces.mono) and composes (Forces.of_union). The 1-5 move only adds tetrahedra, and each new triangle {v, x, y} is forced by the tetrahedron {v, a_0, x, y} from the four gauge triangles {v, a_0, a_j} (forces_move15). Non-vacuity: forces_move15_example applies it on the boundary of the 5-simplex with the ten triangles through a vertex. Scope: for complexes reached from the boundary of the 5-simplex by 1-5 moves, and in general whenever the hypothesis Forces K K.tris T holds. Open, not proven: the 3-3 and 2-4 moves. A proof that stays inside the six vertices of a 3-3 move cannot work: over the 2^18 sets of the 18 triangles on the six vertices, the closure before the move minus the triangle sigma is not contained in the closure after the move in 3744 cases, and the converse fails in 3744; the map that replaces sigma by tau sends 12016 of the 39942 closed local sets to non-closed ones. What holds locally (exhaustive): all 18 mixed triangles are forced before the move iff they are forced after it. Numerical evidence only (scripts/spinfoam/forcechain.py): random sequences of 3-3, 2-4 and 1-5 moves from the boundary of the 5-simplex kept the gauge set forcing in every sampled case; the inverse 4-2 and 5-1 moves lose forcing of the transported set at some locations, though a forcing gauge set was found directly on every such complex sampled. Counterexample for the 3-3 move (numerical, pinned by counterexample_33() in scripts/spinfoam/forcechain.py): on a closed triangulation of the 4-sphere with 48 simplices there is a collapsible forcing gauge set of size E-V+1 that stops forcing after a 3-3 move with the set unchanged (42 triangles left unforced). Random search found such cases in 11 of about 99,000 trials, so forcing is not preserved by 3-3 for every forcing gauge set. Measured in about 162,000 further trials with random minimal forcing sets: T forces after the 3-3 move exactly when the closure of T under the tetrahedra that do not contain the moved triangle sigma already reaches every other triangle (no forcing step needs sigma); the characterization for the 3-3 move is the separate entry LL-0077 (proved in Lean).
- **LL-0077.** Forcing is this library's rule (a tetrahedron with three of its triangles in the set forces the fourth), used to show that the gauge-fixed state sum is 1. Statement: for a 3-3 move K -> K' that replaces the triangle sigma by tau, and T a set of triangles of K that does not contain sigma and forces every triangle of K, T forces every triangle of K' exactly when the closure of T under the tetrahedra of K that do not contain sigma reaches every triangle of K other than sigma (forces_move33_iff, ForcesIn is forcing by an arbitrary set of tetrahedra). The proof splits the tetrahedra into those common to K and K' and the three that contain sigma (resp. tau). If the common closure is complete, one tetrahedron forces sigma (resp. tau) from the mixed triangles. If it is not, a derivation can leave the common closure only through a tetrahedron sigma + c whose three mixed triangles are in it (a full row), and after the move only through a full row for tau; if both exist, a finite lemma on the eighteen mixed triangles (local33_prop, a Boolean statement over eighteen variables checked by the kernel with decide) shows that adding sigma, or tau, forces nothing more, so at most one of the two complexes forces (forcing_dichotomy). Non-vacuity: forces_move33_example applies it to the boundary of the 5-simplex after a 1-5 and a 2-4 move, with a set of fifteen triangles and the move {0,2,3} -> {4,5,6}, every hypothesis checked by the kernel. Wrong-input control: local33_control shows that without a full row of tau-triangles the conclusion of the finite lemma fails. Scope: the 3-3 move only, with the set T unchanged by the move and not containing sigma; the 2-4 move and the inverse 4-2 and 5-1 moves are not covered. Numerical evidence (scripts/spinfoam/forcechain.py, not part of the proof): a collapsible forcing gauge set of size E-V+1 on a 48-simplex 4-sphere triangulation loses forcing under a 3-3 move (so the second condition is not automatic), and in about 162,000 random trials the characterization held in every case.
- **LL-0081.** Forcing is this library's rule (a tetrahedron with three of its triangles in the set forces the fourth), used to show that the gauge-fixed state sum is 1. Statement: for a 2-4 move K -> K' that removes the tetrahedron sigma (shared by the two 4-simplices sigma + p and sigma + q) and adds the edge {p, q}, a vertex a of sigma, and T a set of triangles of K that forces every triangle of K, the set T together with {a, p, q} (the triangle that the gauge rule adds) forces every triangle of K' exactly when the closure of T under the tetrahedra of K other than sigma already reaches every triangle of K (forces_move24_iff). The move keeps all triangles and adds the four triangles {p, q, s} for s in sigma; the tetrahedra before the move are the common ones and sigma, after it the common ones and the six {p, q, s, s'}. If the common closure is complete, K forces trivially and the new triangles are forced one after the other from {a, p, q} and the triangles {p, s, s'}, {q, s, s'} (forces24_of_common). If not, K can leave the common closure only through sigma, when exactly three of its four triangles are in it, and in that case a finite lemma on the sixteen triangles {p, s, s'}, {q, s, s'} and sigma minus a vertex (local24, a Boolean statement checked by the kernel with decide) shows that the new triangles can be added without forcing anything more in K', so at most one of the two complexes forces (forcing_dichotomy24). Non-vacuity: forces_move24_example applies it to the boundary of the 5-simplex after a 1-5 move, with fourteen triangles, a = 0 and the move {0,1,2,3} -> {5,6}, every hypothesis checked by the kernel. Wrong-input control: local24_control shows that without the hypothesis that exactly three triangles of sigma are in the set, the conclusion of the finite lemma fails. Scope: the 2-4 move only, with the triangle {a, p, q} the only one added to T; the 3-3 move is LL-0077, and the inverse 4-2 and 5-1 moves are not covered (numerical evidence in scripts/spinfoam/forcechain.py shows that the transported set can lose forcing there). Numerical evidence, not part of the proof: in about 526,000 random cases (random complexes, random minimal forcing sets, every 2-4 move and every a) the characterization held in every case.
- **LL-0089.** Forcing is this library's rule (a tetrahedron with three of its triangles in the set forces the fourth). A set T is robust for a complex K (Robust K T) if it forces every triangle of K using the tetrahedra of K with any one of them removed. Statement: if T is robust for K, then T together with the four gauge triangles {v, a_0, a_j} of a 1-5 move is robust for the complex after the move (robust_move15). The old triangles are forced as before, because the 1-5 move only adds tetrahedra; the ten new triangles {v, x, y} are forced by the tetrahedron {v, a_0, x, y}, and when that tetrahedron is the removed one, through a fifth vertex z (the triangles {v, x, z} and {v, y, z} by {v, a_0, x, z} and {v, a_0, y, z}, then {v, x, y} by {v, z, x, y}). Non-vacuity: robust_move15_example applies it on the boundary of the 5-simplex, where the ten triangles through a vertex are robust (Robust K0 starK0, checked by the kernel by robustBy with explicit forcing steps for each of the fifteen removed tetrahedra). Scope: the 1-5 move only. Conjecture, not claimed: robust sets stay robust under the 3-3 and 2-4 moves, so that a robust forcing gauge set exists on every complex reached from the boundary of the 5-simplex by forward moves. Numerical evidence only (scripts/spinfoam/robust_check.py (longer runs of the same code)): the gauge set carried along from the boundary of the 5-simplex was robust at every one of 1,104,480 tetrahedra on random complexes, the condition of the 3-3 characterization held at every 3-3 location (38,176 of 38,176), and robustness held after each of 822 consecutive forward moves; robustness implies the conditions of forces_move33_iff and forces_move24_iff only through an unproved lemma (that a robust set never needs the moved triangle), measured at 34,270 of 34,270 3-3 locations.

## Dynamical triangulations: Dehn–Sommerville relations

API map: [Lightlike/DynamicalTriangulations/API-map.md](../Lightlike/DynamicalTriangulations/API-map.md)

| ID | Result | Status | Tier | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LL-0055 | The Dehn–Sommerville relations 2N₃ = 5N₄ and 2N₁ − 3N₂ + 6N₃ − 10N₄ = 0 for closed combinatorial 4-manifolds (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.PL.SComplex.IsClosedCombManifold.two_mul_card_eq`, `Lightlike.PL.SComplex.IsClosedCombManifold.dehnSommerville` in [DehnSommerville.lean](../Lightlike/DynamicalTriangulations/DehnSommerville.lean) |
| LL-0059 | The Einstein–Regge action of dynamical triangulations in terms of N₀, N₄ and χ, and its change under the Pachner moves (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction_eq`, `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction_move`, `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction_move_one_five` in [Action.lean](../Lightlike/DynamicalTriangulations/Action.lean) |
| LL-0062 | The Einstein–Regge action of 3D dynamical triangulations in terms of N₀ and N₃, and its change under the 3D Pachner moves (see note) | proven | established | `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction3_eq`, `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction3_move23`, `Lightlike.DynamicalTriangulations.dtAction3_move14` in [Action3.lean](../Lightlike/DynamicalTriangulations/Action3.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-0055.** N_k is the number of faces with k + 1 vertices of a complex in Lightlike.PL. In every dimension n, a face with n vertices of a closed combinatorial n-manifold lies in exactly two top faces and 2N_{n-1} = (n + 1)N_n; in dimension 4 the second relation follows from the Euler characteristic 0 of the vertex links, which are PL 3-spheres. As checks, the boundary of the 5-simplex is a closed combinatorial 4-manifold with N = (6, 15, 20, 15, 6), computed by the kernel, and two 4-simplices glued along a tetrahedron are not a manifold and violate 2N₃ = 5N₄. These are the combinatorial input of four-dimensional dynamical triangulations; the Einstein–Regge action, causal triangulations and ergodicity of the moves are not formalized here.
- **LL-0059.** For a closed combinatorial 4-manifold the action −κ₂N₂ + κ₄N₄ equals −2κ₂N₀ + (κ₄ − 2κ₂)N₄ + 2κ₂χ, through N₂ = 2N₀ + 2N₄ − 2χ from the Dehn–Sommerville relations (LL-0055). A move with 2 ≤ #σ and 2 ≤ #τ keeps N₀ and χ and changes the action by (#σ − #τ)(κ₄ − 2κ₂), so the 3-3 move leaves it unchanged; the 1-5 move adds one vertex and changes it by −2κ₂ + 4(κ₄ − 2κ₂) (dtAction_move_one_five). Kernel checks: the boundary of the 5-simplex has action −20κ₂ + 6κ₄ (dtAction_sphere), and the formula without the χ term gives −24κ₂ + 6κ₄ there, the wrong value. Not covered: the Lorentzian action of causal dynamical triangulations, which weighs (4,1) and (3,2) simplices differently. As a non-vacuity check, the 1-5 move of the boundary of the 5-simplex with a new vertex changes the action by −2κ₂ + 4(κ₄ − 2κ₂) (sphere7_dtAction_move), and a 2-4 move on the result by 2(κ₄ − 2κ₂), the formula with #σ = 4 and #τ = 2 (sphere7_dtAction_move24).
- **LL-0062.** For a closed combinatorial 3-manifold the Dehn–Sommerville relations give N₂ = 2N₃ and N₁ = N₀ + N₃, so χ = 0 (dehnSommerville3, card_tris, card_edges, euler_eq_zero in DehnSommerville3.lean), and the action −κ₁N₁ + κ₃N₃ equals −κ₁N₀ + (κ₃ − κ₁)N₃. The 2-3 move changes it by κ₃ − κ₁ and the 1-4 move by 3κ₃ − 4κ₁. Checks: after a 1-4 move on the boundary of the 4-simplex a 2-3 move applies and changes the action by κ₃ − κ₁ (dtAction3_S3_14_23); the boundary of the 4-simplex has counts (5, 10, 10, 5) and action −10κ₁ + 5κ₃; two tetrahedra glued along a triangle violate N₂ = 2N₃ and are not a combinatorial manifold (Tests3.lean).

## Colored graphs of group field theory

API map: [Lightlike/GFT/API-map.md](../Lightlike/GFT/API-map.md)

| ID | Result | Status | Tier | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LL-XXXX-e | Colored graphs and the Euler characteristic of their dual complex in dimension 2, checked on the 2-sphere and the torus (see note) | proven | frontier | `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.bubble`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.nBubbles`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.mem_bubble_iff`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.nBubbles_empty`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.even_card`, `Lightlike.GFT.not_nonempty_coloredGraph_fin3`, `Lightlike.GFT.ColoredGraph.twoChi2`, `Lightlike.GFT.twoChi2_theta`, `Lightlike.GFT.twoChi2_torus`, `Lightlike.GFT.badLines_not_proper` in [ColoredGraph.lean](../Lightlike/GFT/ColoredGraph.lean) |

Notes:

- **LL-XXXX-e.** Definitions after Gurau 2010, Section 5: a colored graph of dimension D has vertices of two orientations and lines of D + 1 colors, exactly one line of each color at every vertex, every line joining opposite orientations (ColoredGraph: one fixed-point-free involution per color and an orientation that each involution flips); a p-bubble is a connected component of the subgraph of the lines with colors in a set of size p (bubble: the vertices reachable in #V steps); the dual complex has one k-simplex for each (D - k)-bubble (Theorem 2, eq. (38)). Proved: the computed bubble is the connected component, i.e. the set reachable along lines with colors in S (mem_bubble_iff); the 0-bubbles are the vertices (nBubbles_empty); a colored graph has an even number of vertices, so none exists on three (even_card, not_nonempty_coloredGraph_fin3). For D = 2 the dual has #V triangles, 3#V/2 edges and one vertex for each bicolored cycle, so 2χ = 2(B01 + B02 + B12) - #V (twoChi2): the graph with two vertices and three lines gives χ = 2, the sphere (twoChi2_theta), and a graph with six vertices gives χ = 0, the torus (twoChi2_torus), both by decide +kernel. Wrong model: a vertex with two lines of one color makes the graph not properly colored (IsProper, badLines_not_proper). Not proved: Gurau's Theorem 1 (the p-bubbles are the links of the (n-p)-simplices of the dual) and Theorem 2 (the dual is a normal simplicial pseudo-manifold); that twoChi2 is the Euler characteristic of a closed surface built from the dual (only the face count is formalized); that the Euler characteristic of a connected graph is even. The D = 2 genus statement is standard (ribbon graphs and crystallization theory) and is not in Gurau 2010. Only two examples are computed, not a general theorem.
